title: Year-end checks at a packaging client
learn: Why the receipt date decides the year of a purchase
How to read a PO’s approval box and rate
How to spot red flags in a payments export
do: Flag payments and write one observation

case.role: First-year article assistant on the statutory audit
case.client: Kesari Flexipack Private Limited, a flexible-packaging maker in Chakan, Pune
case.goal: Close the purchase cut-off and stock count papers before the manager’s review

messages: Four bills I picked around 31 March are in the pack, with POs, GRNs and the ledger. Vouch them, then do the stock count sheet.
Manager reviews at 4. Flag anything odd in the payments export too.

documents.title: Internal memo · Year-end cut-off
documents.subject: Year-end cut-off for purchases
body: Goods received at stores up to 31 March 2027 go into 2026–27. Goods received on or after 1 April go into 2027–28, whatever the bill date.
- Stores to send the GRN register for 25 March to 5 April by 6 April.
- Accounts to hold any March bill whose goods have not come in.

documents.title: Purchase policy · Approval limits
documents.subject: Purchase policy
body: ## 4. Approval of purchase orders
Every purchase order is approved in writing before it is sent to the vendor. The approver is decided by the value of the PO before GST:

columns.label: Value of the PO before GST

tasks.title: Vouch the year-end bills
tasks.prompt: Open each bill with its PO, GRN and the ledger. Mark it Fine or Exception, say what is wrong, and note the quantity the stores accepted and the year it belongs to.
hints: Read the day the goods came in before the bill date. The goods decide the year, not the paper.
Check the PO’s approval box and its rate against the bill.

options.label: GSTIN on the bill differs from the vendor master
Rate on the bill differs from the PO

items.label: Bill 1 · Avishkar Polymers
items.note: Bill 1: PO approved, 2,500 kg received on 25 March, booked on 24 March at the PO rate. Fine.

items.label: Bill 2 · Shubh Labh Films Private Limited
items.note: Bill 2: bill dated 30 March, but the film reached our stores on 2 April. The PO says ownership passes on acceptance, so this belongs to 2027–28.

items.label: Bill 3 · Mahalaxmi Adhesives
items.note: Bill 3: the PO for ₹1,47,000 has no approver’s signature. The policy needs the plant head above ₹1 lakh. Exception, even though the goods came in fine.

items.label: Bill 4 · Rangoli Inks and Coatings
items.note: Bill 4: the bill charges ₹386 a kg; the approved PO says ₹362. That is ₹9,600 more before GST. Ask purchase who agreed to the new rate.

tasks.title: Count the stock and work out the variance
tasks.prompt: Tap each bin in the stock room, count what is on the shelf, and fill in the counted quantity, the variance and the variance % against the stock register.
hints: Counted = cartons × per carton + loose. Variance = counted − book.

notes.r3.counted: Three full cartons of 12 and six loose cans. Count the loose ones too.

tasks.title: Scan the payments for red flags
tasks.prompt: Go through the January–March payments. Use the tools to find duplicates, round sums, weekend payments and any vendor that looks linked to an employee. Flag each with its reason.
hints: Turn on Duplicates first, then Match. Flag only the second payment of a pair.

matchWith.label: Match masters
matchWith.title: Vendors that share details with an employee

notes.p07: A round amount with no bill behind it. Ask for the bill or the approval.
notes.p18: Same bill paid twice, three days apart. Get the second one back or adjusted.
notes.p24: Jyotirling Traders is paid into Jyoti Waghmare’s salary account. Raise it with the partner today.
notes.p28: A round amount with no bill behind it. Ask for the bill or the approval.
notes.p33: Paid on a Sunday. Who released it, and why could it not wait?

tasks.title: Calls on cut-off
tasks.prompt: Answer the two questions the manager will ask you about Bill 2.
hints: Read the PO terms on ownership.

questions.text: Bill 2 is dated 30 March, but the film reached the stores on 2 April. Where does this purchase belong?

options.text: 2026–27, because the bill is dated in March
options.why: The bill date does not decide it. The PO says ownership passes on acceptance at stores.

options.text: 2027–28, when the stores accepted the goods
options.why: Acceptance at stores on 2 April passes ownership, so the purchase and the creditor belong to next year.

options.text: Split equally between the two years
options.why: One delivery is not split between years.

questions.text: Which papers show the goods actually reached the factory?

options.why: Stores prepare it when goods are received and accepted.
Security writes it when the truck enters, with date and time.
The supplier writes it; it proves a sale was billed, not received.
It shows what was ordered, before anything arrived.

tasks.title: Put the vouching steps in order
tasks.prompt: Arrange the steps the way you would do them on the file.
hints: Start from the register, end with the client.

steps.text: Pick the bills to vouch from the purchase register around 31 March
Match each bill to its approved PO: item, rate and quantity
Match the bill to the GRN: quantity accepted and date received
Trace the bill to the ledger: amount, account and date booked
List the exceptions and ask the client for reasons

notes.s1: Picking the bills comes first; everything else works on them.
notes.s5: Exceptions go to the client only after you have all of them.

tasks.title: Write the approval observation
tasks.prompt: Build the observation for the management letter from the parts below. Pick the best line for each part.
hints: The criteria line must come from the client’s own policy.

options.text: PO KFPL/PO/26-27/0437 for ₹1,47,000 of adhesive was placed without an approver’s signature.
options.why: States the fact with the PO number and value.

options.text: The adhesive supplier charged more than the PO rate.

options.why: Too vague for a management letter.

options.text: The purchase policy needs the plant head’s approval on every PO above ₹1 lakh.
options.why: This is the client’s own rule, from section 4 of its policy.

options.text: GST law needs every PO to be approved.
options.why: GST law says nothing about PO approval.

options.text: The auditor must approve every PO.
Goods can be ordered without anyone checking the need, the price or the vendor.
options.why: That is the risk the approval is there to stop.

options.text: The bill can never be paid.
options.why: Overstated: the bill can be paid once the PO is ratified.

options.text: Block GRN entry for POs without approval in the system, and get this PO ratified by the plant head.
options.why: Fixes the cause and this instance.

options.text: Stop buying adhesive from this vendor.

freeText.label: Add one line of your own

wrap.text: Good file. Bill 2 is the one the manager will ask about, so keep the gate slip with it. Send me the observation on Bill 3 before you leave.

wrapPartial.text: Most of the file is there. Go through the misses below before anything goes to the client; Bill 2 is the one the manager will ask about.

passNeeds.note: Your bill calls need more right before this passes.

model.intro: Three of the four bills are exceptions. The count shows a small shortage in LDPE and BOPP and two extra cans of adhesive.

rows.issue: Rate ₹24 a kg above the PO

items: Reverse Bill 2 from March purchases and creditors.
Recover or approve the ₹9,600 rate difference on Bill 4.

blocks.text: Always put the gate slip on file with a cut-off exception. It ends the argument.

principles: The goods decide the year, not the bill date.
An unapproved PO is an exception even when the goods are fine.
